solver.kind: blind AI solver B (separate agent, answer-free packet, adversarial rubric)

S077-01.notes: Subject is singular 'decision' (head noun), separated from verb by 'to extend service hours on weekends and holidays'; 'has benefited' agrees. B is the attractor (plural 'holidays' proximity). C puts comma between subject and verb; D dash + plural verb. All seams clean.

S077-02.notes: 'Of the two portraits... the one that hangs in the east wing' is restrictive (identifies which of two); no commas. B/D open a nonessential comma with no closing comma before 'was'; C puts a comma between subject and verb. Adversarial: B would need a closing comma after 'wing' to even be arguable; it lacks one. Seams clean.

S077-03.notes: Compound predicate 'tested ... and replaced' with shared subject 'The engineers'; no comma needed. A (comma before second verb of compound predicate) is the main attractor; SAT convention treats it as wrong. B semicolon not followed by independent clause; C comma splice. Seams clean.

S077-04.notes: 'argued that [clause]' - no punctuation between verb and its that-clause object. A, C, D all insert unnecessary punctuation; C's comma pairs oddly with the later comma before 'rather' but 'that, the treaty's' is still wrong. Seams clean.

S077-05.notes: Nonessential participial phrase 'rediscovered in 1799 ... Rashid' is closed by the comma before 'carries', so it needs an opening comma (B). A lacks the opening comma; C 'which rediscovered' makes the stone the agent (illogical, and verb lacks object); D semicolon fragment. Fact check OK: found July 1799 by French soldiers (Napoleon's expedition) near Rashid/Rosetta; one Ptolemaic decree (196 BCE) in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Greek; key to Champollion's 1822 decipherment. 'rediscovered' is acceptable (it was reused building material). Seams clean.

S077-06.notes: Subject 'The two researchers who first described the tiny freshwater snail in 2019' + verb 'named' - no comma between subject and verb. B is the strongest attractor (comma for readability after the long subject), but it separates subject from verb; C/D add comma between verb and object. Slight momentary ambiguity ('in 2019 named it') is not a real problem. Seams clean.

S077-07.notes: Subject 'The engineer who designed the town's first water tower' + verb 'predicted' + that-clause; no punctuation. A, B, C each insert an incorrect mark. Arithmetic check: 2019 - 104 = 1915, internally consistent. Seams clean.

S077-08.notes: Colon after an independent clause introduces the explanation/specification 'the weather in the narrow window...'. A semicolon needs an independent clause after it (phrase only); B comma is weak/arguably acceptable as an appositive-ish but SAT treats colon as the clearly correct mark - comma creates a run-on-sounding appositive to 'other' and is not standard here; C comma splice. Adversarial on B: 'one thing more than any other, the weather...' - an appositive renaming 'one thing' set off at sentence end by a comma is marginally defensible in casual prose, but the colon is unambiguously best; not blocking.

S077-09.notes: Two independent clauses ('By noon the bakery had sold every loaf of bread' / 'by evening, even the last tray of pastries was gone'); semicolon joins them. A comma splice; C 'which' creates nonsense; D ': and' is nonstandard. Seams clean.
